title: The cascade and specificity
summary: Predict which rule wins when several rules style the same element.

quiz.explain: Both rules match, but a class selector is more specific than a type selector, so green wins even though it is not last.
The selectors are equally specific, so the one written later wins.

quiz.q: Which selector is the most specific?
quiz.explain: Roughly: an id beats a class, a class beats a type. `#main` outranks `p.note`, which has one class and one type.

options: It is not supported by browsers
It overrides normal specificity, so later fixes need more !important
quiz.explain: `!important` jumps the queue. Soon you need it everywhere to beat your own earlier rules. Raise specificity or reorder rules instead.

quiz.q: Which selector would beat `.note` for an element with `id="special"`?
quiz.explain: An id selector beats a class selector, regardless of order.

exercise.task:
Some rules already exist in the style block. Add rules to win the conflicts **without** using `!important`. Work in `index.html`.

- The paragraph with `id="special"` must be red even though it also has class `note`.
- The other `note` paragraphs must stay green.
- Add a second `.late` rule after the existing one so `.late` has a `pink` background.
hints: Two rules with the same specificity are decided by order. A more specific selector wins regardless of order.
Use `#special` to beat `.note`. Put the new `.late` rule below the old one.

checks.name: The #special paragraph is red
checks.hint: Add #special { color: red; } because an id is more specific than a class.

checks.name: Other .note paragraphs stay green
checks.hint: Do not change the .note rule. Target #special instead.

checks.name: The .late element has a pink background
checks.hint: Add a new .late { background-color: pink; } rule after the existing one.

checks.name: !important is not used
checks.hint: Win by specificity and order, not by !important.
